Canterbury's sixth archbishop, Deusdedit, holds a quiet first: no Anglo-Saxon had held England's primacy before him. Born in Wessex under the Saxon name Frithona, Ithamar of Rochester consecrated him at Canterbury in 655 and held the see until his death on 14 July 664. This Catholic Encyclopedia entry of 1913 is frank about how little his nine years left behind.

Only one of his consecrations is certain, Damian of Rochester in 656, and claims about his part in founding Peterborough rest on a disputed charter. His death fell on the same day as Kent's King Erconbert, and Canterbury's St. Peter's porch received his burial. The entry's value lies in its restraint, marking the start of a long line of English archbishops with exactness rather than invention.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vincenzo-de-v:
Vincenzo de Vit was an Italian Latinist who lived from 1810 to 1892. Born at Mestrina near Padua, he studied at Padua, was ordained in 1836, became librarian of Rovigo's Academy of Concordi and canon of its cathedral in 1844. Then, under Rosmini's influence, entered the Institute of Charity at Stresa, where he began revising Forcellini's Latin lexicon.

Needing libraries, he worked at Florence in 1861 and Rome from 1862, returning north each summer. Unlike Forcellini and Furlanetto, he aimed to cover every period and variety of Latin down to AD 568, digesting decadent authors and Church Fathers exactly and giving large space to inscriptions. His Lexicon of All Latinity, a third larger than Furlanetto's edition, was completed in 1879, though its bulk forced him to omit proper names. His Onomasticon reached only the letter P, and no one has finished it.

five-children-and-it:
E. Nesbit sent five children digging in a Kent gravel pit, where they woke the Psammead, a grumpy sand-fairy who grants one wish a day. The children are Cyril, Anthea, Robert, and Jane, with a baby brother called the Lamb. Each wish lasts only until sunset, and each goes wrong in a fresh way.

They wish to be beautiful, to find gold guineas, to have wings, and to be grown up, and undo the damage by teatime. Nesbit tells the mishaps in a dry, funny voice that treats magic as a household nuisance. Five Children and It became a model for later children's fantasy: ordinary children, real tempers, and wishes that teach care in asking.

govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PoliticalMorali:
Hundreds of citizens signed this pledge during the Vietnam era. They refused to pay their federal income taxes voluntarily while American forces were used, in their words, in violation of the Constitution, international law, and the United Nations Charter. The pledge names Vietnam and the invasion of the Dominican Republic. It also charges American indifference to crimes committed in the signers' names.

War tax refusal was a disciplined form of protest: sign, refuse, and accept the penalties. A printed pledge with hundreds of names turned private conscience into public record. The document preserves the movement's legal argument in its own words. It also preserves its moral one, that paying for a war is a choice for which each taxpayer answers.
griboyedov-verstand-schafft-leiden-woe-f:
Chatsky returns to Moscow full of wit and ideals and finds society stupid, corrupt, and ready to call him mad. Alexander Griboyedov's verse comedy Woe from Wit appears here in German translation as Verstand schafft Leiden. Written in 1824, the play became the masterpiece of Russian drama before Chekhov.

Nearly every line of Griboyedov's verse passed into proverb; Russians quote it the way English speakers quote Shakespeare. Famusov's stuffy household, the silent Molchalin, and Chatsky's blazing monologues fill a single ballroom with a whole society. The comedy circulated in manuscript for years because censors feared it. German readers receive a classic whose home audience knows it by heart. Few national literatures rest so much on one play.
hasisadra-s-adventure-essay-7-from-scien:
Thomas Henry Huxley retold the Babylonian flood story in Hasisadra's Adventure, the seventh essay of Science and Hebrew Tradition. Huxley begins with the tale itself: Hasisadra of Surippak dreams of a coming deluge, builds a ship caulked with bitumen, and rides out six days of storm. He sends out a dove, a swallow, and a raven, exactly as Noah would, then sacrifices on a mountain.

The story survives, Huxley explains, on a clay tablet from Assurbanipal's library at Nineveh, copied from a far older original known before 2000 B.C. His point lands quietly: the Hebrew flood narrative has a Babylonian elder brother, and geology and criticism, not mockery, must settle what that means. It is Huxley's science-versus-scripture campaign in miniature.
lectures-on-evolution-essay-3-from-scien:
Thomas Henry Huxley's Lectures on Evolution form the third essay in Science and Hebrew Tradition. Huxley opens with the vast diversity of Nature itself. Just ideas about that system, he says, matter deeply to everyone.

Humans are tiny points in extent and brief in duration, he admits. Still, our past history can be studied with care. He sets out three hypotheses about the history of nature. Evidence, not scripture or guesswork, must judge between them. The essay shows Huxley teaching evolution to a broad public. The lectures were first given to American audiences. Huxley's tour made evolution a headline topic across the Atlantic.
lectures-on-the-english-poets-delivered-:
William Hazlitt delivered his Lectures on the English Poets at the Surrey Institution. The second edition appeared in 1819, and this text was proofed against it. An introductory lecture on poetry in general opens the course.

Hazlitt moves through England's great poets with bold judgments. His lectures helped define the Romantic view of poetry. Feeling, power, and imagination matter more to him than rules. Audiences heard criticism performed like literature itself. These talks remain among the finest short guides to English verse. Chaucer, Shakespeare, and Milton anchor his course. Hazlitt's own prose burns with the gusto he praises.
life-and-habit:
Samuel Butler first published this book in 1878, then revised it. A 1910 edition added a preface by R. A. Streatfeild. Butler inscribed the work to Charles Paine Pauli, his barrister friend. Pauli had criticized the proof sheets of this and earlier books.

Streatfeild notes thirty-three years of change since the book first appeared. Many mighty figures had fallen, and humble ones risen, meanwhile. Butler's title joins two subjects: how life works and how habit shapes it. The book remains a key statement of his thinking about living things. The 1910 reprint followed in 1924 from Butler and Tanner. Butler dedicated his gratitude for Pauli's criticism across many books.
little-dorrit:
Charles Dickens sets this novel around the Marshalsea debtors' prison. His preface to the 1857 edition heads the contents. Book the First, called Poverty, lists thirty-six chapters. Sun and Shadow opens the story in Marseilles heat.

Amy Dorrit appears as the Child of the Marshalsea early. Her father earns the title Father of the Marshalsea. Chapters promise the whole science of government in satire. Fortune-telling, conspirators, and Mrs. Flintwinch's dreams thicken the plot. Bleeding Heart Yard and the lock introduce Marshalsea society. Little Dorrit's party and Mrs. Flintwinch's second dream follow.
martin-chuzzlewit:
Charles Dickens wrote Martin Chuzzlewit, a novel named for its young hero. His preface names greed and selfish pride as the book's core faults. He points to Mr. Pecksniff and to Jonas Chuzzlewit as key cases.

Dickens says Jonas grew cruel from the way he was raised and praised. Vice learned at home, he argues, falls back on the old man at last. The preface also defends the American part of the tale from claims of mere mockery. He also notes how crime in one home can breed crime in the next. The tale's humor sits close to that stern moral thread.
mary-jane-her-visit:
Mary Jane: Her Visit, by Clara Ingram Judson, came out in 1918. Barse and Hopkins printed it in New York and Newark. Frances White drew the pictures, as she did for Her Book.

Mary Jane rides the train to Glenville and explores a farm. She hunts for eggs, gardens with Grandfather, and learns to cook. Odd bundles, a garden thief, and a strawberry social add fun. A picnic at Flatrock comes just before she goes home again. Cousin John's visit and Grandfather's treat break up the farm days. The visit ends with the trip home, rested and full of tales.
meyer-us4798661-gas-generator-voltage-co:
Stanley A Meyer received United States Patent 4,798,661 on January 17, 1989, for a gas generator voltage control circuit. The circuit watches over the cell in his water fuel cell system. It is one of the later filings in his eight-patent family.

The design senses how much gas the cell is making and adjusts the voltage to match. Meyer wanted steady gas flow without wasting power or overheating the cell. The drawings show the sensors, the control loop, and the safety cutoffs. A patent proves a design was new on paper only. An Ohio court found Meyer's claims fraudulent in 1996.
michelangelo-a-collection-of-fifteen-pic:
Estelle M. Hurll edited this volume in the Riverside Art Series, published at Boston in 1900. It gathers fifteen pictures by Michelangelo, plus a portrait of the master. Hurll supplies an introduction and an interpretation for each work. A frontispiece portrait, attributed to Bugiardini, comes from the Uffizi Gallery in Florence.

The pictures include the Madonna and Child, the David, the Moses, and the Pietà. Hurll adds a directory of the works, collateral readings, and a table of the artist's life. She also lists his famous Italian contemporaries. The series aimed to put guided art study into the hands of ordinary readers.
mohammedanism-lectures-on-its-origin-its:
C. Snouck Hurgronje delivered these lectures in the American Lectures on the History of Religions series of 1914 and 1915. The printed volume followed in 1916. Hurgronje was professor of Arabic at the University of Leiden in Holland. His subject is Islam's origin, its religious and political growth, and its present state.

The lecture committee, founded in 1892, brought leading European scholars to American cities. Courses ran in Baltimore, Boston, Chicago, New York, and Philadelphia, among others. Hurgronje had studied Islam in Mecca and advised the Dutch colonial government. His lectures gave American audiences a scholar's survey of a faith then little understood in the West.
mrs-peter-rabbit:
Thornton W. Burgess published this animal tale in 1919, with pictures by Harrison Cady. Peter Rabbit has lost his appetite and feels lonesome. The contents send him on a trip to the Old Pasture. Hooty the Owl and sharp claws threaten the way.

Peter finds strange tracks and meets Little Miss Fuzzytail. Old Jed Thumper gets fooled along the way. Burgess wrote these bedtime tales to teach nature with charm. Each short chapter ends with a hook for the next. The book tells how Peter found a mate, told as soft adventure for young children.
nasa-tm-19630004521-the-explorer-xvi-mic:
Earl C. Hastings, Jr. compiled this NASA memorandum, TM X-824, in April 1963. It gives early results from the Explorer XVI satellite. That craft was built to count hits from micrometeoroids, tiny space grains. This supplement covers January 14 to March 2, 1963.

Hastings reports that thin pressure cells on the craft were punctured. Twenty-four cells of the thinner type had been holed by March 2. Six cells of the thicker type had been holed as well. Rates per square foot per day are given for both kinds. The counts were then matched against rates predicted before launch. Such data told engineers how much shielding real satellites would need.
nasa-tm-19650011719-space-operations-con: Volume 5, number 3 of the Space Operations Control Center satellite situation report is preserved here only as garbled scan text, with no readable body pages. No list of satellites, dates, or figures can be recovered from the hosted sample at all. The title and catalog note alone identify it as a NASA report on orbiting satellites and their current situation in orbit.
nasa-tm-19660002338-nuclear-rocket-simul: Nuclear rocket simulator tests, beginning with a run on flow initiation at thirty-five pounds per square inch with no turbine gas tank pressure, are named in the title of this NASA report. The catalog note adds that a liquid hydrogen run checked operating steps for instruments and data systems. The hosted sample preserves no readable body text, so no author, center, date, or test results can be grounded from it.
nasa-tm-19660009070-a-review-of-fatigue-:
Herbert F Hardrath at Langley reviewed fatigue research across the United States for an international meeting in Munich in June 1965. His scope is work done in government laboratories or under government support. Fatigue is the slow cracking of parts under repeated load. It remains a leading cause of structural failure in aircraft.

Topics in the review, per the catalog note, run from acoustic fatigue to crack growth and detection. Supersonic transport materials and structural fatigue both appear. A national review lets each laboratory see what the others have learned. Hardrath's survey served that purpose at a meeting of the International Committee on Aeronautical Fatigue, where countries compared notes.
nasa-tm-19660022058-effect-of-orientatio:
Ralph G Garlick at Lewis Research Center studied how tungsten crystals turn from ductile to brittle, and how that change depends on the crystal's direction. Tungsten is a very hard, heat-proof metal. Below a certain temperature it snaps instead of bending. Garlick tested single crystals of zone-refined tungsten, pulled along three named directions, in his summary.

Transition behavior proved highly dependent on orientation, he reports. One direction gave a sharp change and the lowest transition point in his tests. Reduction in area of the pulled specimens served as his measure. Direction matters because a crystal's inner planes are not the same each way. Such data guide the use of tungsten in hot, stressed parts.
nasa-tm-19670002001-space-power-system-m:
L. Rosenblum, C. M. Scheuermann, and T. A. Moss, of NASA's Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, prepared this paper for an alkali metal coolants symposium held in Vienna, Austria, in late 1966. It reports tests of whether niobium and tantalum tubing alloys could survive boiling potassium inside a turboelectric space power system.

Eight alloys were screened in sealed reflux capsule tests at very high temperatures, some for up to 10,000 hours. A second test ran a flowing two-phase loop that copied real power system flow and temperature conditions. Alloys containing reactive elements such as zirconium or hafnium resisted corrosion well. Alloys without those elements all showed significant corrosion. The authors link the resistance to those elements binding oxygen into a stable oxide.
nasa-tm-19680001382-the-structure-of-the:
Isadore Harris, of the Goddard Space Flight Center, and Wolfgang Priester, of the University of Bonn in Germany, examine the thermosphere's daily rhythm. The thermosphere is the high, thin layer where satellites drag. Its structure and variations are the paper's twin subjects.

The daily variation, they argue, is the key to understanding the whole layer. It governs the energy balance: heating, heat loss, conduction, and convection. Earlier calculations, from 1962, failed to place the daily density peak at its observed mid-afternoon time. Those attempts left out sideways interaction. Newer wind calculations, driven by pressure differences, are then considered.
nasa-tm-19680026115-resonant-perturbatio:
C. A. Wagner of Goddard Space Flight Center studies resonant perturbations of Earth satellites in this September 1968 report. Some orbits repeat their ground tracks in step with Earth's rotation. Those commensurable orbits feel strong pulls from longitude terms in Earth's gravity field.

Until recently, only roughly one-day resonant orbits were known. Wagner reports resonant effects on orbits repeating only in about two days. A June 1968 survey found two such orbits with along-track perturbations over one hundred kilometers. Twelve other satellites should show effects over one kilometer. Tracking them over their resonant beat periods could reveal valuable detail about Earth's high-order gravity field. Those details refine orbit prediction for all satellites.
nasa-tm-19700026484-an-analysis-of-the-p:
The Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston issued this internal note on June 16, 1969. It analyzes what the Saturn 5 launch vehicle could still do if two engines failed. The study covers both the remaining performance and how the huge rocket would behave in flight with two of its first stage engines out.

Discussion splits into vehicle performance first, then vehicle dynamics case by case. The failure cases pair the center engine with one control engine, and two control engines in opposed positions. Other cases lose two neighboring control engines at once, or one after the other partway through the burn. Each pairing steers and steadies the rocket differently, so each earns its own treatment.
nasa-tm-19710018396-tesseral-resonance-o:
B. E. Lowrey wrote this NASA preprint, numbered X-554-71-198, on a surprise in the orbit of IMP-4, also called Explorer 34. The satellite flew a highly eccentric orbit, looping far from Earth and back. Its time of closest approach, perigee passage, was being shifted by a resonance with Earth's gravity field.

The abstract traces the shift to the third harmonic of the field, the part describing its lumpiness at that scale. The perturbation swings the perigee time by about nine minutes over a period of roughly two hundred forty days. Lowrey notes the resonance arose because the orbital period nearly matched a simple fraction of Earth's rotation period. He suggests the effect can test current values of those harmonics, and that other eccentric orbits should show it too.
our-farm-of-four-acres-and-the-money-we-:
Miss Coulton's Our Farm of Four Acres tells how two women took a tiny farm and made it pay. By this 1860 printing the little book had reached its twelfth London edition. The preface answers critics in detail: yes, the first cow's legs were strapped, and she knocked man and pail down with her side anyway, until her calf was parted with. The landlord, by agreement, kept gates and buildings in repair; a stream, not hedges, bounds the meadows.

The women churned butter four hours at a time, turn and turn about, until practice cut the work to three quarters of an hour. Nearly eighteen months on, they report themselves as satisfied as ever with their profits. Pitied for never resting, they quote Poor Richard: leisure is the time for doing something useful. It is a founding text of back-to-the-land self-sufficiency.
pareto-manuale-economia-politica-1919-it:
Pareto restated his economics compactly in the Manuale di economia politica, here in its 1919 Italian printing. The manual gives his mature theory in short compass. Ophelimity, his coinage for the satisfaction a good gives, replaces the looser term utility. Indifference curves map how a buyer trades one good against another.

From those curves he builds toward the Pareto optimum, the best balance his system allows. The Italian text stands as a documentary original, since no public domain English translation exists. Students use the manual as the clearest door into his economics. Its appendix on math drew praise and complaint alike. The compact force is pure Pareto.
peck-s-compendium-of-fun-comprising-the-: The hosted sample stops at the front matter of Peck's Compendium of Fun, the title page and the start of the contents, with no sketches visible. The title page names George W. Peck, editor of Peck's Sun of Milwaukee, and calls the book the choicest gems of wit, humor, sarcasm, and pathos of America's favorite humorist. It was published at Chicago in 1886, and the contents run alphabetically from "About Hell" through dozens of short comic pieces.
polly-of-pebbly-pit:
Lillian Elizabeth Roy wrote Polly of Pebbly Pit, published in 1922 as one of her long Polly series. Which had already taken its heroine to New York, abroad, and into a business venture. Roy dedicates the book to her friends Sarah and Bryan Battey. The scene shifts west: a farm in Pebbly Pit, a momentous letter, and preparations for the unknown bring city girls to a Colorado ranch country they do not understand.

Contents promise the series' reliable mixture: the servant problem solved, unpleasant surprises, harrowing details, a little scheme that worked, and the slow acclimation of the city girls. A dance at Bear Forks, a trip into the wilderness, a blizzard on Grizzly Slide, and a night in a cave supply the adventure. Roy's Polly books taught competence as fun; here the lesson is ranch life, learned the hard way, in snow.
rig-veda-americanus-sacred-songs-of-the-:
Daniel G. Brinton edited these sacred songs of the ancient Mexicans as number eight of his Library of Aboriginal American Literature, in 1890. The hymns carry a gloss in Nahuatl, and Brinton adds a paraphrase, notes, and a vocabulary. A picture shows Xippe Totec, god of silversmiths, in full costume, for hymn fifteen.

Brinton's preface says the series furnishes materials for study rather than finished studies. He calls the texts the most ancient authentic record of American religious lore, and names the set Rig Veda Americanus after the sacred hymns of the Aryans. His translation, he warns, is offered with the utmost reserve, so hard are the mystic chants.
romance-of-the-rabbit:
Francis Jammes tells the life of a rabbit in this tale, in Gladys Edgerton's authorized translation from the French, dated 1920. Book one opens amid thyme and dew, where Jean de la Fontaine Rabbit hears the hunt and climbs a path of soft clay. He fears his own shadow as the heather flees behind him.

His eyes, set on the sides of his head, nearly run him into the twelfth milestone between Castétis and Balansun. The dogs lose his scent, and on the road to Sauvejunte he meets a horse and covered cart. The sorry nag drags its cart in a jerky gallop, its skeleton quivering at every leap, a great machine that frightens him.
roughing-it:
Mark Twain calls Roughing It a personal narrative, not a proud history and not a deep study. It records, in his phrase, several years of varied wandering, and it aims to help a resting reader pass an idle hour. Yet he admits that facts stew out of him whether he wants them to or not. The facts concern the rise, growth, and peak of the silver-mining fever in Nevada, which he saw on the ground with his own eyes.

Twain jokes that he would give worlds if he could keep his facts in, but the more he seals the sources, the more he leaks wisdom. He asks the reader for patience rather than claiming he is in the right. The first chapter turns to his brother, appointed Secretary of Nevada, and to Twain's envy of him.
saratoga-and-how-to-see-it: R. F. Dearborn wrote Saratoga and How to See It, illustrated and dated 1872, with a cover price of twenty-five cents. The pages shown here carry a full notice for Drs. Strongs' Remedial Institute, on Circular between Spring and Philadelphia streets. The institute, established in 1855 for the special treatment of lung, female, and various chronic diseases, is praised as unsurpassed for beauty of location and access to the principal springs.
some-remarks-on-the-tragedy-of-hamlet-pr:
Some Remarks on the Tragedy of Hamlet, Prince of Denmark, written by Mr. William Shakespeare, came out without a name in 1736 and is now ascribed to Thomas Hanmer. The Augustan Reprint Society issued it in September 1947 at 75 cents, with a first note by Clarence D. Thorpe. The copy was reprinted from the British Museum's, by leave of its trustees.

The essay opens with a complaint that the art of judging books has been much abused. Most folk, it says, take such judgment to mean fault-finding, and call a man a critic when he is set to blame and slow to praise. A true critic, in the right sense, works to set all beauties in the best light. He touches faults no more than he must, shows how they may be shunned, and tries to fix a right taste.
speech-of-john-hossack-convicted-of-a-vi:
John Hossack speaks in his own defense in a printed speech. The American Anti-Slavery Society issued it at New York in 1860. A court at Chicago had found him guilty. Joseph Stout of Ottawa shared that verdict. Both men aided the rescue of a fugitive slave. A deputy marshal held the man at Ottawa. Judge Drummond fined Hossack one hundred dollars. Ten days in jail went with the fine.

The headnote gives Hossack's life in brief. He was a Scotch baker who had lived in Quebec. He moved to Ottawa, Illinois, some twenty years back. He helped build the Illinois and Michigan Canal. He rose as a grain dealer of good name. In court he owns no sense of guilt. He came as a lad from the Old World's harsh rule. He sought a shore where men of toil stand free.
t-mann-konigliche-hoheit:
Mann's fairy-tale prince appears in his original language in Koenigliche Hoheit, the German text of Royal Highness. Klaus Heinrich of the little state of Grimmburg lives inside ceremony until love and American money crack the shell. Behind the charm stands Mann's serious theme: how art and representation shape modern life.

Elegant and ironic, the novel treats its prince's uselessness as a kind of artistry awaiting a purpose. The heiress Imma brings candor and capital in equal measure. Mann keeps the tone light while the questions about duty deepen underneath. German readers can savor the courtly prose exactly as written. The book charms first and argues afterward, a rare order of operations for its author.
taboo-a-legend-retold-from-the-dirghic-o:
James Branch Cabell's Taboo, printed at New York by Robert M. McBride and Company in 1921, calls itself a legend retold from the Dirghic of Saevius Nicanor, with prolegomena, notes, and a preliminary memoir. The edition was limited to nine hundred and twenty numbered copies, one hundred of them signed by the author.

A Latin motto warns that it would have been better not to write, since silence is always safe. Cabell frames his satire as the work of an obscure old author. A mock-scholarly memoir and introduction complete the frame. The piece had first appeared in The Literary Review. It returns here by leave of its editors. The game is classic Cabell: a small, elegant fable about what may not be said, wrapped in learned fooling.
the-art-of-the-exposition-personal-impre:
Eugen Neuhaus of the University of California gives his own readings of the Panama-Pacific International Exposition's art in this 1915 volume: its building scheme, sculpture, mural work, color, and other fine aspects. Neuhaus chaired the western advisory committee and sat on the fair's San Francisco jury for fine arts.

A publisher's note, dated at San Francisco on May 1, 1915, says the pages grew from talks Neuhaus gave his students through the year. Given as evening lectures at the university and repeated before groups across California, his account stirred such demand that only print could meet it. The fair itself is saluted on the dedication page as a great work of peace.
the-beautiful-necessity-seven-essays-on-:
Claude Bragdon, a fellow of the American Institute of Architects, published seven essays in 1922 under a line from Emerson about building altars to a beautiful necessity. Bragdon dated his opening from Rochester, New York, in April 1922. Other Bragdon books on architecture and higher space are listed.

Contents name the art of architecture first, then unity and polarity, changeless change, and the bodily temple. Latent geometry, the arithmetic of beauty, and frozen music close the set, followed by a conclusion. The titles alone show Bragdon's aim: to join building design with number, form, and spiritual ideas drawn from theosophy.
the-beginnings-of-new-england-or-the-pur:
John Fiske published lectures in 1892 on New England's beginnings and the Puritan theocracy, viewed against civil and religious liberty. A 1654 line from Edward Johnson stands on the title page. Fiske dedicated the book to three classmates by name.

In his preface Fiske says the chapters began as lectures given at Washington University in St Louis in May 1887. He repeated them in Portland, Oregon, and in many cities from Boston to San Francisco. He leaves out many details of formal history to trace an outline of principles at work from settlement down to the revolution of 1689, drawing also on Brooks Adams.
the-continental-monthly-vol-1-no-4-april:
April 1862 brings the fourth number of The Continental Monthly, devoted to literature and national policy. Its lead piece covers the war between freedom and slavery in Missouri, sketching the start of the rebellion in that state and how the army dealt with it.

The writer warns readers up front that no one can write the history of his own times with full fairness. Men act in the scenes they live in, and friends' fortunes color their judgment, so history written in its own day is always partisan history. He offers his sketch as the record of one class of people sure of their duty. He leaves final judgment on the causes to later writers who will see how the struggle ends.
the-continental-monthly-vol-5-no-3-march:
March 1864 brings the third number of volume V of The Continental Monthly, devoted to literature and national policy. Its lead piece is the third of Hon. Robert J. Walker's letters on American finances and resources, dated from Half Moon Street, Piccadilly, London, on December 3, 1863.

Walker grants that war wastes wealth, drains labor from industry, and harms a nation's material interests. Yet he argues the gains will outweigh the losses. Slavery caused the rebellion, he says, and its end will rebuild the Union on free labor. Willing work by educated freemen, he holds, yields far more than forced work by slaves. He turns to the census of 1860 to compare yearly output per head in slave states and free states.
the-continental-monthly-vol-iii-no-v-may:
May 1863 brings the fifth number of volume III of The Continental Monthly, devoted to literature and national policy. Its lead piece, The Great Prairie State, introduces Illinois to readers the writer suspects know less of it than of the tiny republic of San Marino.

Illinois has lately been abused, the writer says, for the misdeeds of some of her sons, which only makes her loyal friends love her more. Seen from New York, she is one great green prairie, its flat spread broken by rivers and by rail lines that serve as causeways through spring and winter mud. Her scattered farmers work black soil so rich that neglect leaves crops rotting in the fields. Her rough, thriving towns favor the tavern and the race course over church and lyceum.
the-fertility-of-the-unfit:
W. A. Chapple, a doctor, wrote The Fertility of the Unfit to argue that folk classed as unfit were having more children than the rest. A preface by Rutherford Waddell frames the book's claims in stark terms.

Waddell calls the growth of crime a dark cloud over all lands and scolds the practice of freeing convicts after fixed terms. Chapple, he says, takes a far more drastic cure than set terms or long detention. The book stands as a record of the eugenics thought of its day: fear of crime and poverty turned into a plan to stop whole classes from having children.
the-forfeit: Ridgwell Cullum wrote The Forfeit as a western novel, printed at New York under a copyright of 1917. Only the front matter and contents are present here. The chapter heads name Rainbow Hill Valley, a hanging bee, outland justice, a polo club race, a home-coming, and an epic battle, which points to a ranch tale of feud and force. Cullum's past books named on the title page include The Night Riders and The Trail of the Axe. No chapter text can be read here.
the-gospels-in-the-second-century-an-exa: W. Sanday wrote The Gospels in the Second Century. It was printed in London in 1876. Its subtitle calls it an examination of the critical part of Supernatural Religion. Sanday was rector of Barton-on-the-Heath and a late fellow of Trinity College, Oxford. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page, a dedication note, and the start of a contents list. Sanday had hoped to inscribe the book to Dr. Pears of Repton, his old head master. A telegram named the day of Pears's funeral first.
the-grand-canyon-of-arizona-how-to-see-i: George Wharton James wrote The Grand Canyon of Arizona: How to See It. Only front matter is present here. It is a Project Gutenberg header. The header gives notices on copyright laws. It tells readers to keep the file whole. It honors the volunteers who made the text. It notes that Dianne Bean of Prescott Valley, Arizona scanned the text. No page of the guide itself is present. Its routes, views, and advice for seeing the canyon cannot be told from what is here.
the-herd-boy-and-his-hermit: Charlotte M. Yonge wrote The Herd Boy and His Hermit, with a heading in the record dated 1900. Verses by Southey about Henry of Windsor stand at the front. The contents list chapters such as In the Moss, The Snow-Storm, Over the Moor, A Sporting Prioress, Mother and Son, On Derwent Banks, The Hermit, and Henry of Windsor. Only the title page, verses, and contents are present here, so the story itself does not appear. A second record in the library carries the same title page, verses, and contents.
the-highland-fling-and-how-to-teach-it:
Prof. Grant, of 485 Main St., Buffalo, N.Y., wrote The Highland Fling and How to Teach It, Book No. 2, dated November 1892 and printed at Buffalo. Grant explains that in teaching fancy dances, faster progress comes from forming exercises that match the movements to be done. The dance uses a hopping movement, with hands and arms set against the feet.

Letters mark the feet throughout: R for right and L for left. Exercise number one has the dancer hop four times on the left foot, then four on the right, then left again, then right while turning fully around. The pattern repeats starting on the other foot. Grant calls that exercise the foundation for the fling, meant to be practiced with care.
the-history-of-rome-book-i-the-period-an: Theodor Mommsen wrote The History of Rome, Book I, on the period before the abolition of the monarchy, translated with the author's sanction by William Purdie Dickson, D.D., LL.D., professor of divinity in the University of Glasgow. The pages present add a preparer's note explaining how foreign words, sounds, and letters from Latin, Greek, Gothic, and Phoenician are marked in plain text. Only the title page and preparer's note are present here, so the history itself does not appear.
the-house-fly-and-how-to-suppress-it:
Farmers' Bulletin No. 1408 from the United States Department of Agriculture takes up a household pest that also threatens public health. L. O. Howard, chief of the Bureau of Entomology, and entomologist F. C. Bishopp wrote it, and the government issued it in Washington in April 1925, then revised it in November 1926. The opening pages argue that flies signal unclean conditions and poor waste handling, since insects that breed in filth can carry disease germs onto exposed food.

Readers learn which flies turn up indoors, where the house fly breeds, and how it survives the winter. Later sections turn practical, covering screens, fly papers, poisons, sprays, and traps for shutting flies out and catching them. The strongest stress falls on stopping breeding altogether, through better built and better kept stables and cleaner disposal of the substances flies breed in.
the-open-door-and-the-portrait:
Margaret O. Wilson Oliphant wrote two stories of the seen and the unseen, The Open Door and The Portrait. The narrator of The Open Door took the house of Brentwood, near Edinburgh, on his return from India. His son Roland, pale from Simla, rides his pony to the High School each morning, as Dr. Simson advised.

Brentwood stands on a rich slope between the Pentland Hills and the Firth, above a glen with a paper mill stream. The family finds the view endlessly fresh after India's arid plains. A sister record carries the same opening text word for word; readers meet the household before the strange events begin. Oliphant sets her ghostly tale in calm domestic detail.
the-opium-habit:
A compiled volume on the opium habit, with suggestions as to the remedy, gathers first-hand accounts of addiction and cure. A line from Coleridge stands at the front, begging that his wretchedness be made public after his death so some good might come of the example. The contents promise De Quincey's Confessions of an English Opium-Eater and opium reminiscences of Coleridge.

The introduction says the book was compiled chiefly for opium-eaters themselves. It also addresses doctors, general readers, and moralists. Other pieces compare opium and alcohol, tell of insanity and suicide after giving up morphine, and outline an opium cure. Case after case shows the cost of the habit and the hard road back.
the-pit:
Frank Norris's The Pit, a story of Chicago, was published at New York in 1903 and dedicated to his brother Charles Tolman Norris. Front matter names the principal figures. Curtis Jadwin is a capitalist and speculator, and Sheldon Corthell is an artist. Landry Court is a broker's clerk, Samuel Gretry a broker, and Charles Cressler a grain dealer. Laura Dearborn, her sister Page, and their aunt Mrs. Emily Wessels complete the list.

A note then sets out Norris's planned Trilogy of the Epic of the Wheat. The Octopus, a story of California, treats the production of wheat. The Pit treats its distribution through Chicago. The Wolf, a story of Europe, was to treat its consumption as bread in a western European village. The three novels would stand apart in plot, linked only by one crop's passage from sowing to eating.
the-prose-works-of-jonathan-swift-d-d-vo: Volume III of Jonathan Swift's Prose Works, in Bohn's Standard Library, gathers his Writings on Religion and the Church as their first volume. Temple Scott edited the set, with a biographical introduction by W. E. H. Lecky. The title pages are dated 1898, and a portrait after Frances Bindon fronts the volume. The pages provided reach only the start of Scott's preface, on religious thought in the eighteenth century; Swift's church tracts themselves are not shown.

Volume IV of Swift's Prose Works continues the Writings on Religion and the Church as their second volume. Temple Scott edited the Bohn's Standard Library set, printed by George Bell and Sons in 1898. The contents begin with the tracts on the Sacramental Test. A sibling record holds Volume III, the first volume of the same church writings. The leaves at hand stop at the contents head, so none of Swift's arguments are present.
the-silence-what-it-is-and-how-to-use-it: David V. Bush wrote The Silence: What It Is and How to Use It. The pages shown here give that title matter and a publisher's list. The list advertises a series of six booklets by Bush at twenty-five cents each. The Silence stands fourth among them. Other titles treat prosperity, visualization, and suggestion. No chapter of The Silence itself appears in the portion shown.
the-south-pole-an-account-of-the-norwegi: Roald Amundsen's account of the Norwegian Antarctic expedition in the Fram, 1910 to 1912, was translated from the Norwegian by A. G. Chater. The pages present here carry his dedication, dated at Uranienborg on August 15, 1912. It honours the brave little band who promised at Funchal to stand by him. A contents list runs from the history of the South Pole through depot journeys and winter at Framheim. It ends at the start for the Pole, so the narrative itself does not appear.
the-story-of-a-candy-rabbit: Laura Lee Hope's Make Believe story of a candy rabbit was published by Grosset and Dunlap in New York, illustrated by Harry L. Smith. Only the title pages and publisher's lists are present here. The lists place the book among the Make Believe stories. The Sawdust Doll and the White Rocking Horse stand beside it. The Lamb on Wheels and the Bold Tin Soldier follow. A Bobbsey Twins list comes after. The rabbit's own adventures do not appear.
the-tale-of-peter-rabbit:
The Saalfield Publishing Company of Akron issued this Peter Rabbit in 1916, with illustrations by Virginia Hibert rather than Beatrix Potter's own drawings. Potter's story opens with four little rabbits named Flopsy, Mopsy, Cotton-tail, and Peter. They live with their mother in a sandy bank beneath a big tree's roots.

From that homely opening grows the best known of all the Peter Rabbit adventures, in which a disobedient young rabbit tests his mother's warnings. This edition shows how widely Potter's tale had spread by 1916, reaching American children through a different publisher and a different artist's hand. The familiar names and home burrow anchor every later escape and scrape.
the-velveteen-rabbit:
Margery Williams tells how a toy becomes real in The Velveteen Rabbit, illustrated by William Nicholson and published by Doubleday at Garden City, New York. The Rabbit begins splendidly, fat and bunchy with a spotted brown-and-white coat, real thread whiskers, and ears lined with pink sateen. He sits in the top of the Boy's Christmas stocking with holly between his paws.

For two hours the Boy loves him best of all the presents, ahead of nuts, oranges, a toy engine, and a clockwork mouse. Then aunts and uncles arrive, tissue paper rustles, and the Rabbit is forgotten among newer gifts. An illustrations list promises the Skin Horse's story, anxious times, a fairy flower, and a joyful ending.
the-village-sunday-school-with-brief-ske:
John C. Symons wrote The Village Sunday-School, revised by Daniel P. Kidder and published in New York in 1850 for the Sunday-School Union of the Methodist Episcopal Church. An illustration names its three scholar subjects: James, Thomas, and George. Symons's preface disclaims any pretension to authorship and admits many defects in his production.

The narratives, he says, are substantially true, though names of persons and places are changed. He sends the sketches out to encourage pious teachers in duties that can feel discouraging. His own labour in a Sabbath-school drew strength from these same facts. If even one devoted teacher gains encouragement, he writes, his purpose will be more than answered.
the-world-s-best-poetry-volume-08-nation:
Bliss Carman edited The World's Best Poetry, and volume eight, National Spirit, opens with an essay on studying poetry. Francis Hovey Stoddard wrote that essay. He quotes Bacon on how clever, ignorant, and wise men treat studies. Study alone, Bacon argued, does not teach its own use. Wisdom beyond study comes from observation, Stoddard notes.

Stoddard reflects on years of studiousness and its emptiness. Mere learning, he suggests, leaves the deepest lesson outside itself. The essay introduces an anthology of patriotic verse. Poems sorted by national feeling fill the volume's plan. Readers get both a defense of poetry and a guide to reading it well.
un-ga-res-statement-of-president-rodrigo:
Rodrigo Duterte, president of the Philippines, addressed the United Nations General Assembly for the first time at its seventy-fifth session in 2020. The session was held largely online because of the COVID pandemic, so he spoke by video from Manila. His drug war had drawn years of world criticism by then.

Duterte defends his campaign against drugs and rejects what he calls foreign meddling in it. He also raises the South China Sea ruling won by his country and pledges to uphold it. The statement shows a combative leader using the UN stage to answer his critics at home and abroad.
what-germany-thinks-or-the-war-as-german: Only the title page and contents are present here, so the chapters themselves do not appear. Thomas F. A. Smith wrote What Germany Thinks in 1915. He had taught English at the University of Erlangen and knew the country well. The contents list chapters on the causes of the war, mobilization, and the fall of the Social Democrats. Other chapters cover Belgium, tales of cruelty, and the writing of hate. Readers see his plan for showing the war through German eyes, but not his text.
what-was-it:
Fitz-James O'Brien, an Irish born writer in New York, wrote this tale for Harper's Magazine in March 1859. Its full name adds the words 'A Mystery' to the stark first line. O'Brien died young, in the Civil War, with a small set of tales that still stand tall.

Men in a boarding house seize a beast that no eye can see, and bind it fast. It is strong, it fights, and it can be felt and heard, yet the gaze passes through it as through air. The tale is the first of the unseen beast, a root of a vast line of later tales.
your-united-states-impressions-of-a-firs: Arnold Bennett wrote these impressions of a first visit to the United States, published in 1912 with pictures by Frank Craig. Pages present here hold the title page, a contents list, and a list of illustrations, but no chapter text. Chapters promise first nights, streets, the Capitol, transit, hotels, sport, theatre, and citizens. Listed pictures show Fifth Avenue, Wall Street, and Chicago scenes. Bennett's judgements themselves stay absent from these pages.
